paras: The Stroud restaurant dynamiting was an attack in September 1903 in which unknown persons set off dynamite at the restaurant of James Wadkins, a Black man, in Stroud, Oklahoma Territory, while Black patrons were inside. The blast wrecked the floor or the whole building and broke windows; most reports said no one was hurt, and the suspects who were arrested were released. White papers in Oklahoma, Kansas, Missouri and Wyoming reported it as a sequel to the town's expulsion of its Black residents two years earlier.

According to a dispatch from Stroud printed in the Wichita Daily Eagle, Black residents had been driven out of the town two years before, and it had been "free from them" until about three weeks before the attack, when Wadkins opened a restaurant. The same report said public sentiment was against him, so strongly that the town's bakers and butchers refused to sell to him. A Chandler correspondent of the Guthrie Daily Leader likewise wrote that the last Black resident had been driven out two years earlier and that only recently had "any member of the race" been admitted. A later item from Stroud added that Wadkins had been warned to leave the town, "where negroes are unpopular," and had declined to move.

The attack came at night while a number of Black people were gathered in the restaurant, which the Eagle described as "a high old time in Wadkins' joint" and the Leader as a celebration. In the Eagle's account someone exploded a stick of dynamite under the shack, demolishing the floor and breaking the windows, while a Guthrie wire report said "unknown parties" had placed dynamite under the floor and that the blast demolished the building. The Laclede Blade instead said unknown persons threw a stick of dynamite into the restaurant. Those inside fled; the Eagle and the Leader reported that none were injured, whereas the Blade said several were "knocked insensible."

Several arrests followed, but the suspects were released because, in the Eagle's words, guilt "could not be proved." No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage. The Eagle reported that the Black patrons said they would come back, but added that "in the present state of public opinion it would be dangerous for them to do so." Wadkins himself was quoted in the Blade as declaring that he "can't be blown out of town," though the coverage does not show whether he stayed.

All of the coverage found came from white papers, beginning with the Wichita Daily Eagle on September 25 under the headline "FLED IN TERROR." The Guthrie Daily Leader ran its Chandler special in an "Oklahoma News" column the next day. A Guthrie wire version reached the Wyoming Tribune in Cheyenne on September 28 as "NEGROES WERE BLOWN UP" and the Butler Weekly Times in Missouri on October 1 as "Negro Meeting Dynamited." The Laclede Blade, also in Missouri, printed a short Stroud item on October 3 under "Dynamite Don't Frighten Him," which centered on Wadkins' refusal to leave.

None of these papers condemned the attack or the earlier expulsion, which each report gave as settled background. The Eagle framed the danger to returning Black people as a matter of "public opinion," and the wire report described the town as having been "free from them" until recently. No account of the attack in the Black press was found, including in Oklahoma Black papers of the period.

Reports differ on the date: the Eagle's Stroud dispatch of September 24 placed the explosion on "Monday night," which would be September 21, while the Guthrie wire dated September 24 and the Leader's Chandler special dated September 26 both said "last night." The Eagle's dispatch, datelined from Stroud and the most detailed, gives the most specific date. Accounts also differ on injuries and method: the Eagle and the Leader reported no one hurt, the Eagle and the wire placed the dynamite under the building, and the Blade said it was thrown inside and knocked several people unconscious.

reader.title: Stroud restaurant dynamiting
bases: Unknown persons exploded dynamite under or in a Black man's restaurant while Black patrons were inside, in a town that had driven out its Black residents two years earlier and where he had been warned to leave (A1, A2, A5).

A Stroud dispatch (A1), a separate Chandler special (A2), a Guthrie wire (A3, A4) and a later Stroud item (A5) agree that dynamite wrecked a restaurant where Black people were gathered, though they differ on injuries, method and date.

accounts.label: Stroud dispatch (Wichita Eagle)
accounts.gist: On Monday night someone exploded a stick of dynamite under Wadkins' shack while Black patrons were inside, wrecking the floor and windows; none were hurt; suspects arrested and released.

accounts.label: Chandler special (Guthrie Daily Leader)
accounts.gist: A charge of dynamite demolished Wadkins' restaurant 'last night' while Black people celebrated there; all escaped injury; suspects released.

accounts.label: Guthrie wire
accounts.gist: Unknown parties placed dynamite under the floor of a restaurant where 'colored people' were celebrating; the building was demolished; numerous arrests, all released.

accounts.label: Stroud item, Oct. 1 (Laclede Blade)
accounts.gist: Wadkins was warned to leave and refused; unknown persons then threw dynamite into his restaurant, knocking several Black people insensible; he said he could not be blown out of town.

Guthrie wire under 'NEGROES WERE BLOWN UP' and 'Negro Meeting Dynamited', describing the town as having been 'free from them'.
Headlined 'Dynamite Don't Frighten Him', centering Wadkins' defiance; described Stroud as a town 'where negroes are unpopular.'
